text: Marea Dvīpa. From guidance to proposal. This is a walk through one piece of work: how we help a small hospitality business take its bookings back from the platforms. It runs from the first audit, through the published guide and the quote builder, to a proposal a client can click through, and the tool we use to make the next one.

It started with one house. The Beam House is a holiday let with a hot tub and a story behind most of its objects. We built its direct-booking site in a day: a live calendar with seasonal, midweek and gap-night prices, a floor-plan tour with thirty object stories, a short film rendered from the owner's photographs, and an assistant that knows the house and can pick dates. Then we took apart a well-marketed hotel site in Brighton. Six hundred and forty-four kilobytes of HTML on one page. Forty-four scripts and sixty-two stylesheets. Forty-four of sixty-nine images with no alt text. And not one price on the page. The marketing layer was excellent. The engineering layer was neglected. That gap is the offer.

Every engagement starts with the audit, and the audit starts with facts. We fetch the page with a plain client, run a small script over the raw HTML, and read what the server actually sends. Fourteen technical checks: page weight, alt text, skip link, labelled forms, reduced motion and dark theme, an accessibility statement, language, structured data, consent, the booking hand-off, on-page pricing, reasons to book direct, and self-service for the guest. Then eight questions a guest arriving from Airbnb expects answered in the first minute: the rating and review count, the price and total, live dates, the cancellation terms, a map, who the host is, protected payment, and whether it all works on a phone. The script gives us the numbers. The two checklists turn them into a ranked list of fixes.

Everything we learned became the Business Website Guide, published on our own domain. It opens with the thesis: the guest should book with the house, not with the platform. The offer has three parts, bought together or separately: an audit, written guidance, and the design and build. Then why it matters: price and availability on the page, a reason to book direct, speed and trust, and accessibility, which in the UK is a duty under the Equality Act. The audit checklist is interactive. Pick a preset and see how a real site scores, or score your own and the page remembers it. The benchmark teardown shows the hotel's numbers beside what was worth copying. Our baseline follows: one HTML file, no framework, every photo with alt text, a keyboard calendar, light and dark from one set of tokens, and consent before any analytics load. The design principles keep the restraint: photography leads, corners stay subtle, nothing hides behind a hover. The features menu filters by purpose, each with when to use it and what the owner must supply. The case study shows The Beam House before and after. Then the three packages, the eight-step process, a go-live checklist you can tick, and the measures we review at thirty days.

The second room is the platform analysis. Of every thousand pounds a guest pays for a stay, the owner keeps between seven hundred and fifty and a thousand, depending on the channel. The calculator shows it: drag the price of a stay and every channel updates with what the owner keeps or what the guest is charged, with the fee basis on hover. The fee table marks which figures are official and which come from third-party guides, because Booking dot com, Vrbo and Sykes block automated reading of their owner pages. We audited one Brighton listing on each platform the same way we audit a client. Vrbo's page is the heaviest at eight hundred and fifty-seven kilobytes and a hundred and ten scripts. Sykes is the lightest and has the richest structured data. Only Airbnb has a skip link. None offers a dark theme. From that came the parity checklist, the owner's edge, and five changes to our own guidance, including one we had missed: calendar sync with the platforms, which the channel managers include and we now do too.

The quote builder is the form a client fills in. Who they are, where they are listed, what matters most, and roughly what they take in a year. Then the level of service: the audit at four hundred and fifty pounds, the direct-booking site at two thousand four hundred, or the signature site at four thousand eight hundred. Features marked included come with the package; anything else carries its own price, and languages, polish rounds and additional houses take a quantity. Care after launch is a monthly plan, and the payment schedule offers five percent off for paying in full. The quote updates as they go. If we have audited their site in the last sixty days, the audit fee comes off the build in full. When they send it, the quote is saved to our store where their account allows, and otherwise comes to us as text they paste into their reply. Every price in the proposal you are about to see can be rebuilt here, to the pound.

Here is the process on a real client. The Grove Collection runs characterful holiday homes in Brighton and the Dordogne. We audited the hub and the two property sites it links to. The craft is there: a light page, a skip link, reduced motion, every image with alt text, and real reviews quoted with names and dates. Five of fourteen technical checks pass, and two of the eight guest questions are answered. What is missing is the moment of booking. No price anywhere. Check availability leaves for a Lodgify domain that answers every automated request with a bot check. Google Tag Manager loads with no consent banner. No map, no FAQ. The concierge idea, Plan My Stay, runs on an external site. The measured table puts the hub beside its property sites and an Airbnb listing. Then come three options, each shown as a working mock-up of the Coach House page, drawn in the Grove Collection's own cream, green and terracotta. Option B is the one we recommend: one collection site, booked direct, with a live calendar, Stripe on their own domain, two-way calendar sync, and waiting lists for the two houses still to open. Three thousand four hundred and fifty pounds plus thirty-five a month. The compare table shows what each option adds. The payback slider sets their yearly income against Airbnb's host fee. The recommendation and next steps close it.

Option A keeps WordPress and Lodgify and tunes what they have: the review count beside the name, a price card with a one-line cancellation policy, a perks strip, a map and FAQ, a consent banner and the lodging schema. One thousand four hundred and fifty pounds. It fixes six of the eight findings; booking still completes off-site.

Option C is the signature collection: everything in B, plus Plan My Stay brought in-house as an assistant that knows each house and can check dates, an interactive tour with the stories behind the rooms, a film for each live house, offers and gift vouchers, and two rounds of polish. Six thousand pounds plus ninety-five a month for hosting and care. Every one of these figures comes from the same price list as the quote builder.

On our side, the Proposal Studio turns an audit into a proposal in an afternoon. The form on the left is the whole configuration: client, brand colours and faces for the mock-ups, the fourteen checks, the eight questions, what is already right, the houses with their rates and stories, the three options, the compare table and the payback assumptions. Paste the audit script's output and the measured table and nine of the fourteen checks fill themselves. The preview on the right is the finished proposal, live, with every mock-up working. Save it as a file and it drops straight onto marea-dvipa.uk under proposals, or save the configuration to the store for the next revision.

Everything is live. The guide at marea-dvipa.uk slash web. The quote builder at slash quote. And the first proposal at slash proposals slash grove-collection. The audit is four hundred and fifty pounds, credited in full against a build started within sixty days. Marea Dvīpa. Distinctive places deserve a website that books them.
